title: UNIT 1: CHEMICAL REACTIONS AND STOICHIOMETRY
notes:
✓ Chemical reactions → Conversion of reactants into products.

The unit also covers chemical equations, balancing, types of reactions, oxidation-reduction, molecular and formula masses, mole concept, chemical formulas and stoichiometric calculations.

◆ MAJOR CALCULATIONS
✓ Mole-mole relationships
✓ Mass-mass relationships
✓ Mass-volume relationships
✓ Volume-volume relationships
✓ Limiting and excess reactants
✓ Theoretical yield, actual yield and percentage yield.

title: 1.1 Introduction
notes:
✓ Physical change → No new substance is formed.
Examples: melting ice, evaporation, powdering sugar.

✓ Chemical change → One or more new substances with different compositions are formed.
Examples: rusting, burning, rotting food, fermentation.

✓ Chemical reaction → A process in which reactants are converted into products.

◆ COMMON EVIDENCE OF A CHEMICAL REACTION
✓ Formation of a new substance
✓ Color change
✓ Temperature change
✓ Production of heat or light.

title: 1.2 Chemical Equations
notes:
✓ Chemical equation → A representation of a chemical reaction using chemical symbols and formulas.

Reactants → Products

✓ Reactants → Written on the left side.
✓ Products → Written on the right side.

◆ PHYSICAL-STATE SYMBOLS
(s) → Solid
(l) → Liquid
(g) → Gas
(aq) → Aqueous solution.

◆ MEANINGS OF A CHEMICAL EQUATION
✓ Qualitative meaning → Identifies reactants and products.
✓ Quantitative meaning → Gives relative amounts of particles, moles or masses.

Example:
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O

✓ A chemical equation must represent a possible reaction, use correct formulas and be balanced according to the law of conservation of mass.

title: 1.2.1 Writing Chemical Equations
notes:
◆ STEPS
1. Write the reaction in words.
2. Replace names with correct chemical formulas.
3. Write reactants on the left and products on the right.
4. Add state symbols when needed.
5. Balance the equation.

◆ DIATOMIC ELEMENTS IN ELEMENTAL FORM
H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.

◆ EXAMPLE
Hydrogen + Nitrogen → Ammonia
H₂ + N₂ → NH₃

✓ Balanced equation:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

title: 1.2.2 Balancing Chemical Equations
notes:
✓ Balancing follows the Law of Conservation of Mass → Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

✓ To balance an equation → Make the number of atoms of each element equal on both sides by changing coefficients, not subscripts.

◆ METHODS
✓ Inspection method
✓ Least Common Multiple (LCM) method
✓ Algebraic method.

◆ EXAMPLE
H₂ + N₂ → NH₃
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

title: 1.3 Types of Chemical Reactions
notes:
◆ FOUR MAJOR TYPES
✓ Combination → A + B → AB
Two or more substances form one product.
Example: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

✓ Decomposition → AB → A + B
One compound breaks into simpler substances.

✓ Single displacement → A + BC → AB + C
One element replaces another element in a compound.

✓ Double displacement → AB + CD → AD + CB
Two compounds exchange ions.

title: 1.3.1 Combination Reactions
notes:
✓ Combination reaction → Two elements, two compounds, or an element and a compound combine to form one product.

General form:
A + B → AB

◆ EXAMPLES
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃
Fe + S → FeS

✓ Combination reactions are also called synthesis or composition reactions.

title: 1.3.2 Decomposition Reactions
notes:
✓ Decomposition reaction → A single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

General form:
AB → A + B

Decomposition may occur by heating, electricity or other forms of energy.

◆ EXAMPLE
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂

→ Decomposition is essentially the reverse pattern of combination.

title: 1.3.3 Single-Displacement Reactions
notes:
✓ Single-displacement reaction → One element replaces another element in a compound.

General form:
A + BC → AB + C

◆ EXAMPLES
Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu
Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu

✓ A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.

title: 1.3.4 Double-Displacement Reactions
notes:
✓ Double-displacement reaction → Two compounds exchange their positive and negative ions to form two new compounds.

General form:
AB + CD → AD + CB

◆ EXAMPLE
AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃

✓ A precipitate may form when one product is insoluble.

◆ ANOTHER EXAMPLE
BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl.

title: 1.4 Oxidation and Reduction Reactions
notes:
✓ Redox reaction → A reaction involving simultaneous oxidation and reduction with electron transfer.

✓ Oxidation → Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number.
✓ Reduction → Gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation number.

◆ EXAMPLE
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Zn loses electrons → Oxidized.
Cu²⁺ gains electrons → Reduced.

◆ MEMORY AID
OIL → Oxidation Is Loss.
RIG → Reduction Is Gain.

title: 1.4.1 Oxidation Number / Oxidation State
notes:
✓ Oxidation number → Represents the apparent charge or electron change of an atom in a compound.

◆ IMPORTANT RULES
✓ Free elements → Oxidation number = 0.
✓ Monatomic ion → Oxidation number = ion charge.
✓ Oxygen is usually −2.
✓ Oxygen in peroxides → −1.
✓ Oxygen in superoxides → −1/2.
✓ Hydrogen is usually +1 when bonded to nonmetals and −1 in metal hydrides.
✓ Fluorine → −1.
✓ Sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound → 0.
✓ Sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion → Ion charge.

title: 1.4.2 Oxidizing and Reducing Agents
notes:
✓ Oxidizing agent → Causes another substance to be oxidized and is itself reduced.

✓ Reducing agent → Causes another substance to be reduced and is itself oxidized.

◆ EXAMPLE
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
Zn → Reducing agent and is oxidized.
Cu²⁺ → Oxidizing agent and is reduced.

title: 1.4.3 Balancing Redox Reactions by Oxidation Number
notes:
◆ BASIC STEPS
1. Assign oxidation numbers.
2. Identify the elements oxidized and reduced.
3. Determine the increase and decrease in oxidation numbers.
4. Make total increase equal total decrease.
5. Use the resulting numbers as coefficients.
6. Balance remaining atoms and check the equation.

✓ Non-redox reactions → No electron transfer and oxidation numbers remain unchanged.
Examples include many neutralization and double-displacement reactions.

title: 1.5 Molecular Mass, Formula Mass, Mole Concept and Chemical Formulas
notes:
✓ Molecular mass, formula mass and molar mass → Used to determine amounts of substances and percentage composition.

✓ Molecular mass (MM) → Sum of atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule.

✓ Formula mass (FM) → Sum of atomic masses in one formula unit, mainly used for ionic compounds.

◆ EXAMPLES
H₂O = 2(1) + 16 = 18 amu.
NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 amu.

title: 1.5.2 Mole Concept
notes:
✓ Mole → Amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles.

◆ AVOGADRO'S NUMBER
Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ particles/mol.

✓ Molar mass → Mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in g/mol.

◆ IMPORTANT RELATIONSHIPS
n = m/M
m = nM
N = nNₐ
n = N/Nₐ

where:
n = moles
m = mass
M = molar mass
N = number of particles.

title: 1.5.3 Percentage Composition
notes:
✓ Percentage composition → Percentage by mass of each element in a compound.

Formula:
% element = (mass of element in 1 mol compound / molar mass of compound) × 100%

For an element appearing n times:
% element = (n × atomic mass / molar mass of compound) × 100%.

✓ Total percentages of all elements → 100%.

title: 1.5.4 Empirical and Molecular Formulas
notes:
✓ Empirical formula → Simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

✓ Molecular formula → Actual number of atoms in one molecule.

◆ EXAMPLES
Benzene → Empirical CH; molecular C₆H₆.
Glucose → Empirical CH₂O; molecular C₆H₁₂O₆.

◆ EMPIRICAL FORMULA STEPS
1. Convert each element's mass or percentage to moles.
2. Divide all mole values by the smallest value.
3. Multiply by an integer if necessary to obtain whole numbers.

◆ MOLECULAR FORMULA
n = molecular molar mass / empirical formula mass
Molecular formula = empirical formula × n.

title: 1.6 Stoichiometry
notes:
✓ Stoichiometry → Quantitative relationships between reactants and products.

◆ STOICHIOMETRY IS BASED ON
✓ Correct chemical formulas.
✓ Conservation of mass.
✓ A balanced chemical equation.

✓ A balanced equation provides mole, particle and mass relationships.

◆ MAIN TYPES
✓ Mole-mole
✓ Mass-mass
✓ Mass-volume
✓ Volume-volume.

title: 1.6.1 Molar Ratios
notes:
✓ Coefficients in a balanced equation → Give the mole ratio of reactants and products.

◆ EXAMPLE
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

Mole ratio:
1 mol N₂ : 3 mol H₂ : 2 mol NH₃.

The same equation represents particle ratios and, after using molar masses, mass relationships.

◆ EXAMPLE
28 g N₂ + 6 g H₂ → 34 g NH₃.

title: 1.6.2 Mass-Mass Relationships
notes:
✓ Mass-mass calculation → Determines the mass of one substance from the mass of another.

◆ BASIC METHOD
1. Balance the equation.
2. Convert the given mass to moles.
3. Use the mole ratio from the equation.
4. Convert the required moles to mass.

◆ KEY FORMULAS
n = m/M
m = nM

→ Mass-ratio and mole-ratio methods can be used.

title: 1.6.3 Volume-Volume Relationships
notes:
✓ At STP (0 °C and 1 atm) → One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L.

✓ Molar volume at STP → 1 mol gas = 22.4 L.

✓ Avogadro's Law → Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

At the same conditions:
Gas volume ∝ Number of moles.

✓ For volume-volume problems → Use the coefficients of the balanced equation as gas-volume ratios.

title: 1.6.4 Mass-Volume Relationships
notes:
✓ Mass-volume problems → Connect the mass of one substance with the volume of a gaseous substance.

◆ STEPS
1. Balance the equation.
2. Convert the given mass to moles.
3. Use the mole ratio.
4. Convert gas moles to volume using 22.4 L/mol at STP.

◆ USEFUL RELATIONSHIPS
n = m/M
V = n × 22.4 L at STP.

title: 1.6.5 Limiting and Excess Reactants
notes:
✓ Limiting reactant → Reactant consumed first; determines the maximum amount of product.

✓ Excess reactant → Reactant present in more quantity than required and remains after the reaction.

◆ IDENTIFYING THE LIMITING REACTANT
1. Convert each reactant to moles.
2. Use the balanced equation to calculate the possible product from each reactant.
3. The reactant producing the smaller amount of product is the limiting reactant.
4. Product amount is based on the limiting reactant.

✓ Excess remaining = Initial amount − Amount consumed.

title: 1.6.6 Theoretical, Actual and Percentage Yield
notes:
✓ Theoretical yield → Maximum amount of product calculated from the limiting reactant.

✓ Actual yield → Amount of product actually obtained experimentally.

✓ Actual yield is usually less than theoretical yield because of side reactions, incomplete reactions and product loss.

◆ PERCENTAGE YIELD
% yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%

✓ Higher percentage yield generally indicates a more efficient reaction.

title: UNIT 1 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ Chemical reaction → Reactants are converted into products.

✓ Physical change → No new substance is formed.
✓ Chemical change → New substance(s) are formed.

✓ Chemical equation → Symbolic representation of a chemical reaction.
✓ Balancing → Equalizes atoms on both sides according to conservation of mass.

◆ TYPES OF REACTIONS
✓ Combination → A + B → AB.
✓ Decomposition → AB → A + B.
✓ Single displacement → A + BC → AB + C.
✓ Double displacement → AB + CD → AD + CB.

◆ REDOX
✓ Oxidation → Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number.
✓ Reduction → Gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation number.
✓ Oxidizing agent → Is reduced.
✓ Reducing agent → Is oxidized.
✓ Non-redox → No oxidation-number change or electron transfer.

◆ MASS AND MOLE CONCEPT
✓ Molecular mass → Sum of atomic masses in a molecule.
✓ Formula mass → Sum of atomic masses in a formula unit.
✓ Molar mass → Mass of one mole, g/mol.
✓ Mole → 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
✓ Avogadro's number → 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
✓ n = m/M.
✓ N = nNₐ.

◆ CHEMICAL FORMULAS
✓ Empirical formula → Simplest whole-number ratio.
✓ Molecular formula → Actual number of atoms in a molecule.
✓ % Composition → (mass of element / mass of compound) × 100%.

◆ STOICHIOMETRY
✓ Stoichiometry → Quantitative relationships between reactants and products.
✓ Mole ratio → Obtained from coefficients of a balanced equation.
✓ STP molar volume → 22.4 L/mol.
✓ Avogadro's Law → Equal gas volumes at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
✓ Limiting reactant → Consumed first and determines product amount.
✓ Excess reactant → Remains after the limiting reactant is consumed.
✓ Theoretical yield → Maximum calculated product.
✓ Actual yield → Experimentally obtained product.
✓ Percentage yield → (Actual yield / Theoretical yield) × 100%.

✓ KEY IDEA → Always balance the chemical equation before performing stoichiometric calculations.
